text:
sam: Quick check — we need to pick an approach for service auth: edge gateway enforcement (Envoy + RBAC filters) vs an external policy agent (OPA) that services call. Pros/cons?

lina: high level: gateway gives single place to block, easier to reason for ingress. OPA gives richer policies and versioned rules, but adds runtime hops.

derek: +1 to gateway for perf. We saw 12–20ms p95 extra when we added an external call in the demo last month. For high-throughput paths that's painful.

maya: OPA benefits: can express hierarchical org/project rules and reuse same policies for internal admin tools. Also good for canarying policy changes.

sam: tradeoff list I'm thinking: latency, failure modes, policy expressiveness, rollout complexity, telemetry. Anything missing?

lina: developer ergonomics — where do app teams author the rules? If OPA, they can push policy bundles. With gateway, they'd need central PR process or a policy service API.

derek: failure modes: gateway-offline = global outage risk. OPA-offline per-service could just degrade auth checks differently. We need clear fallback semantics.

maya: what about hybrid: simple RBAC (allow/deny by route and role) in gateway, heavy attribute-based rules in OPA called asynchronously for audits and slow-path decisions?

sam: hybrid seems promising. Proposal sketch: 1) Gateway enforces coarse-grained routing and token validation + project/org claim checks. 2) Services query local OPA (sidecar) for fine-grained decisions where needed, with a default fallback behavior. 3) Central policy registry for bundles + CI checks.

lina: fallback semantics: gateway denies by default if OPA unreachable for a fine-grained check? that could break flows. Maybe gateway allows if coarse check passes but flags the request for audit if OPA is unavailable.

derek: prefer safe-fail closed for admin endpoints, open for user-facing low-risk ops. We should classify endpoints into RISK_BUCKET = {HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW} and set default fallback per bucket.

maya: example defaults: HIGH -> deny if fine-grained check fails/unavailable, MEDIUM -> allow but emit alert, LOW -> allow.

sam: ops question: sidecar OPA means more moving parts per pod. Ops cost vs centralized OPA cluster. Thoughts?

lina: sidecar gives locality and zero network hop, but increases memory. Central OPA cluster simplifies ops but needs caching. Both ok if we provide a policy packaging and rollout system.

derek: telemetry: gateway should emit token-level decisions and latency. OPA decisions should be tagged with policy bundle version so we can correlate regressions to policy changes.

maya: we also need a migration plan for existing API keys and RBAC roles. Suggested steps: 
- export current key->role mappings
- backfill org/project claims into tokens for a trial window
- run policy in "shadow" mode for 2 weeks and compare denies

sam: can we draft a short RFC with: decision matrix, hybrid architecture diagram, fallback policy per risk bucket, rollout plan & metrics to watch?

lina: I'll start an RFC draft. Action: Lina to create draft by EOD Thu. Derek to run a perf microbenchmark of gateway-only vs sidecar OPA on friday. Maya to assemble risk bucket mapping for endpoints. Sam will draft telemetry/event schema.

security-bot: Reminder: run the automated policy lint and reachability tests before enabling any global deny-by-default policies.

derek: +1 to that. Also, include a canary policy bundle pipeline: unit tests -> staging bundle -> 5% rollout -> 100%.

maya: question: API key scoping — do we prefer project-scoped keys (short-lived) or org-wide keys? Ops wants fewer tokens to rotate. Product wants easier per-product scoping.

sam: proposal: default to project-scoped keys for new tokens, allow tenant/ org-wide keys via request + approval flow (longer TTL, auditable). Document rotation rules: auto-rotate project keys every 90 days, org keys every 30 days with MFA for issuance.

lina: also add a migration path: map legacy keys to proxy tokens that carry org/project claims until apps can validate directly.

derek: implementation detail: token exchange at edge: accept legacy key, mint short-lived claim-bearing token (kid header) and forward. That keeps internal services simple.

maya: OK. That covers most concerns. TL;DR: go hybrid (gateway coarse + local policy for fine grained), risk-bucketed fallbacks, project-first key policy, shadow-run before deny-by-default.

sam: thanks — Lina will post RFC link when ready. If anyone wants to be on reviewer list ping Lina. :thumbsup:
